# 1 Maccabees Chapter 11 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, 1 Maccabees 11 | **Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Council Notes

Chapter 11 presents the treacherous end of Alexander Balas and the complex dealings of Jonathan with Demetrius II and then young Antiochus VI. The Demetrius privilege letter (vv.30-37) follows directly from chapter 10's Demetrius letter, confirming and specifying grants. The Antioch rescue narrative (vv.44-51) is among the most dramatic scenes in the book. Jonathan's single-handed rally after near-rout (vv.71-73) echoes biblical warrior narratives.

**Key term rulings:**
- "scheming by treachery" (v.1) — preserves the author's moral framing
- "slandered him" (v.11) — preferred over "was false about him" (too archaic); covers the Greek ἐσυκοφάντησεν
- "Ladder of Tyre" (v.59) — proper toponym retained; a coastal escarpment
- "Trans-Euphrates" (v.60) — standard modern designation for "beyond the River"
- "golden brooch" (v.58) — as in ch.10; consistent with SOPHIA ruling
- Jonathan's mourning rite (v.71): "tore his clothes, put earth on his head" — preserved exactly; biblical mourning convention

---

**1** The king of Egypt gathered a great army, as numberless as the sand on the seashore, and many ships, for he was scheming by treachery to seize Alexander's kingdom and add it to his own.

**2** He marched into Syria with friendly overtures, and the people of the cities opened their gates and went out to meet him, because King Alexander had commanded them to do so, as Ptolemy was his father-in-law.

**3** But as Ptolemy entered each city, he installed a garrison.

**4** When he came near Azotus, they showed him the burned-out temple of Dagon and the ruins of Azotus and its suburbs, with bodies strewn about — those whom Jonathan had burned in the war, piled up along his route.

**5** They told the king what Jonathan had done, hoping to discredit him, but the king kept silence.

**6** Jonathan met the king at Joppa with full honor; they greeted each other and lodged there.

**7** Jonathan accompanied the king to the river called Eleutherus, then returned to Jerusalem.

**8** King Ptolemy seized the coastal cities as far as Seleucia-by-the-Sea, all the while devising evil plans against Alexander.

**9** He sent envoys to King Demetrius, saying: "Come, let us make a treaty; I will give you my daughter — the one Alexander now has — and you shall reign over your father's kingdom.

**10** For I regret having given her to Alexander, for he sought to kill me."

**11** He slandered Alexander because he coveted his kingdom.

**12** He took his daughter away from Alexander and gave her to Demetrius; and Ptolemy broke with Alexander, and their enmity was brought into the open.

**13** Ptolemy entered Antioch and put on the crown of Asia; thus he wore two crowns — the crown of Egypt and the crown of Asia.

**14** King Alexander was in Cilicia at that time because the people of that region were in revolt.

**15** When Alexander heard this, he came against Ptolemy to make war; Ptolemy led out his army, met him with a strong force, and put him to flight.

**16** Alexander fled to Arabia to seek refuge there, and King Ptolemy was exalted.

**17** Zabdiel the Arab cut off Alexander's head and sent it to Ptolemy.

**18** But King Ptolemy died three days later, and the garrisons in the fortresses were destroyed by those within the fortresses.

**19** Demetrius became king in the one hundred and sixty-seventh year.

**20** In those days Jonathan mustered the men of Judea to attack the citadel in Jerusalem, and they built many siege engines against it.

**21** Some lawless men who hated their own nation went to the king and reported that Jonathan was besieging the citadel.

**22** The king was angry when he heard it; as soon as he heard it, he came to Ptolemais and wrote to Jonathan ordering him to stop the siege and to come to him immediately.

**23** When Jonathan heard this, he ordered the siege to continue; he selected some of the elders of Israel and some priests and took a risk.

**24** He took silver, gold, clothing, and many other gifts and went to the king at Ptolemais, and he found favor in the king's eyes.

**25** Though certain lawless men of his nation brought accusations against him,

**26** the king treated Jonathan just as his predecessors had; he honored him in the sight of all his friends,

**27** confirmed him in the high priesthood and all his other previous honors, and had him registered as one of the king's chief friends, first rank.

**28** Jonathan petitioned the king to exempt Judea from tribute and to transfer the three districts to Judea, promising three hundred talents in return.

**29** The king agreed and wrote letters to Jonathan about all these things:

**30** "King Demetrius to his brother Jonathan and to the nation of the Jews, greetings.

**31** We are sending you a copy of the letter we wrote to Lasthenes our kinsman concerning you, so that you may know it.

**32** King Demetrius to Lasthenes his father, greetings.

**33** We have determined to show favor to the nation of the Jews, who are our friends and who honor their obligations toward us, because of the goodwill they bear us.

**34** We hereby confirm to them the territory of Judea and the three districts of Aphaerema, Lydda, and Ramathaim, which were added to Judea from Samaria, together with all their dependencies, for all who offer sacrifice in Jerusalem — in lieu of the royal revenues that the king previously received from them annually from the produce of the land and from the fruit of the trees.

**35** As for the other dues that henceforth belong to us — the tithes and tolls owed to us, and the salt pits, and the crown taxes — we release all these to them.

**36** Not one of these provisions shall be annulled from this time and forever.

**37** Take care, therefore, to have a copy of this made and given to Jonathan, to be placed on the holy mountain in a conspicuous place."

**38** When King Demetrius saw that the land was quiet before him and no one resisted him, he dismissed all his forces, each man to his own place, except for the foreign mercenaries he had recruited from the islands of the nations; and so all the veteran troops of his predecessors came to hate him.

**39** Now there was a man named Trypho who had previously been on Alexander's side. Seeing that all the army was grumbling against Demetrius, he went to Imalkue the Arab, who was raising Antiochus the young son of Alexander,

**40** and pressed him, saying: "Hand Antiochus over to me, that he may become king in his father's place." He told him all that Demetrius had done and the hatred his troops bore him; and he stayed there many days.

**41** Jonathan sent a request to King Demetrius to remove the garrison of the citadel from Jerusalem and the troops from the strongholds, for they were constantly fighting against Israel.

**42** Demetrius sent back: "Not only will I do this for you and your people, but I will greatly honor you and your people when the opportunity presents itself.

**43** For now, do me this service and send me men to fight for me, for all my forces have mutinied."

**44** Jonathan sent three thousand valiant men to Antioch; they came to the king, and the king was overjoyed at their arrival.

**45** The people of the city — about a hundred and twenty thousand — had gathered together and wanted to kill the king.

**46** The king fled into the palace while the city's people seized the main streets and began to attack.

**47** The king called on the Jews for help; they rallied to him at once, spread out through the city, and that day killed about a hundred thousand men.

**48** They set the city on fire, seized much plunder that day, and rescued the king.

**49** When the people of the city saw that the Jews had gained control of the city, their courage failed and they cried out to the king in supplication:

**50** "Give us terms and make the Jews stop fighting against us and the city."

**51** The king laid down his weapons and made peace. The Jews were honored before the king and before all in his kingdom, and they returned to Jerusalem with rich plunder.

**52** Thus King Demetrius sat secure on his throne, and the land was quiet before him.

**53** But he broke all his promises, estranged himself from Jonathan, and did not repay him for the services rendered, treating him with great harshness.

**54** After this, Trypho returned, and with him the young Antiochus; he was crowned and took the diadem.

**55** All the forces Demetrius had dismissed rallied to Antiochus; they fought against Demetrius, and he fled and was routed.

**56** Trypho captured the elephants and took possession of Antioch.

**57** The young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan: "I confirm you in the high priesthood and appoint you over the four districts, and you are to be one of the king's friends."

**58** He sent him golden vessels and a dinner service, and gave him the right to drink from golden vessels, to wear purple, and to wear a golden brooch.

**59** His brother Simon he appointed governor from the Ladder of Tyre to the borders of Egypt.

**60** Jonathan set out and traveled through the cities of Trans-Euphrates; all the Syrian forces joined him as allies. He came to Ashkelon and the people of the city received him with honor.

**61** From there he went to Gaza, but the men of Gaza shut their gates against him; he besieged it, burned its suburbs, and plundered them.

**62** The men of Gaza appealed to Jonathan, and he gave them his right hand; he took the sons of their rulers as hostages, sent them to Jerusalem, and continued on through the country as far as Damascus.

**63** Jonathan heard that the generals of Demetrius had come with a large army to Kedesh in Galilee, intending to remove him from his position.

**64** He went to meet them, leaving his brother Simon in charge of the country.

**65** Simon encamped against Beth-zur, fought against it many days, and blockaded it.

**66** They appealed to him for terms; he granted the request, but then expelled them from the city, which he seized and placed under garrison.

**67** Jonathan and his army encamped beside the waters of Gennesareth; early in the morning they marched to the plain of Hazor.

**68** There in the plain the army of the foreigners met them; the enemy had laid an ambush in the hills while their main force advanced to meet Jonathan head-on.

**69** The men in ambush burst from their positions and joined battle; all those with Jonathan fled —

**70** not one remaining except Mattathias son of Absalom and Judas son of Chalphi, commanders of the forces.

**71** Jonathan tore his clothes, put earth on his head, and prayed.

**72** Then he turned back against them in battle and routed them, and they fled.

**73** When those who had fled saw this, they turned back and joined him; together they pursued the enemy as far as Kedesh, to their camp, and encamped there.

**74** About three thousand of the foreigners fell that day; and Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.
